headline: High-risk default filesystem and shell overlap: Open Interpreter can read/write the whole user filesystem while gpt-engineer writes project files, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a user-specified project directory and has no self-isolation by default; Open Interpreter can read the filesystem and clipboard, so attacker-controlled project content can be reinterpreted as instructions. This is a plausible default pathway, though not as direct as a shared MCP channel.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter opens or summarizes files created by gpt-engineer without provenance filtering, injected instructions can steer tool use.
IF the shared project directory contains adversarial prompt text, gpt-engineer output can become an instruction source for Open Interpreter.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate directories.
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents.
Require a human to review any file before Open Interpreter reads it.
Use a provenance prefix for machine-generated files.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tagging before cross-agent ingestion.

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-engineer touches generated source code and can write files, while Open Interpreter can read the entire user filesystem and has broad network egress. If both run on the same machine, sensitive local files can flow into Open Interpreter outputs or model calls, creating exfiltration risk beyond the code project.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter is pointed at the same machine account as gpt-engineer, local secrets reachable on disk can be read.
IF Open Interpreter forwards file contents to a configured model provider, those contents can leave the machine.
mitigations: Run each agent under a separate OS user.
Restrict Open Interpreter to a dedicated working directory.
Remove secrets from the shared machine before running either agent.
Disable network egress for the Open Interpreter session.
requires-engineering: enforce filesystem allowlists at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and Open Interpreter also modifies git state. Because gpt-engineer shares state via the project directory and Open Interpreter shares state via the filesystem, concurrent writes can corrupt files or git history in default use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory, simultaneous edits can overwrite each other.
IF Open Interpreter commits or rewrites git state while gpt-engineer is generating files, repository history can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Do not run both agents on the same working tree.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Use separate git branches per agent.
Take a quick backup snapshot before concurrent work.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer produces code and Open Interpreter can execute shell commands and act on filesystem contents, so Open Interpreter may treat generated artifacts as authoritative and perform irreversible actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, making downstream mistakes likely in default workflows.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter executes commands derived from gpt-engineer output without manual review, incorrect code can be run.
IF generated files include destructive shell snippets, Open Interpreter can carry them out as the invoking user.
mitigations: Require manual review before execution.
Run Open Interpreter in dry-run or confirmation mode.
Separate code generation from execution into different sessions.
Use a throwaway test environment first.
requires-engineering: add a verification step that checks generated commands against policy.

E_compliance.rationale: gpt-engineer is scoped to a project directory and generated source code, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine. That mismatch can move broader local data into a tool with broader network egress, creating a compliance gap around retention and residency even though no specific regulated class is named.
conditions: IF regulated or sensitive local files are present on the machine, Open Interpreter can access them outside the narrower project scope.
IF model-provider logging retains prompts, local file contents may be retained outside the intended workspace.
mitigations: Keep regulated data off the shared machine.
Use a dedicated workspace with minimal data.
Review provider retention settings before use.
Document which files may be accessed by Open Interpreter.
requires-engineering: enforce residency and retention controls in the orchestrator.
